newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire rebels take key town of Kindu, U.N. source.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels take key town of Kindu, U.N. source.

text.p: Zaire rebels seized the strategic eastern town of Kindu and foreign aid workers fled a major eastern refugee camp for fear of rebel attack, aid agency and U.N. sources said on Friday.

A U.N. source said the rebels captured Kindu and its airport on Thursday but in Kinshasa a Defence Ministry official told Reuters that Kindu, a transport hub and base for army operations in the war zone, remained in army hands.

The U.N. source added that all 2,000 Zairean troops in Kindu fled without a fight after extensively looting the town and were heading westwards towards the town of Katako-Kombe, 170 km (100 miles) away.
A regional military source said rebels were clearing landmines from Kindu airport and the town centre.
The Kinshasa official accused the rebels of announcing the fall of the town to sow panic and confusion.
Kindu, a heavily-fortified transport hub on the Zaire River, had the northernmost working station on a rail line to South Africa. It also had a large airport used by the military.

The aid officials said an immediate evacuation of all expatriates had been ordered from Tingi Tingi, 260 km (160 miles) northeast of Kindu after camp leaders were warned that the camp would be attacked by another rebel force on Friday night.
Aid workers said Zairean troop reinforcements and mercenaries arrived on Friday from the city of Kisangani to Tingi Tingi, backed by warplanes and helicopter gunships.

Michelle Quintaglie, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme, said: "We have reports that the refugee populations have started to move from Tingi Tingi. We have advised our staff to return to Kisangani because of security concerns."
"The situation on the ground is apparently tense."
Tingi Tingi has some 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees who fled earlier rebel advances.
The regional military source said rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Friday returned from exploratory peace talks in South Africa and headed for his headquarters in the Zairean town of Goma.
Some 500 Rwandan Hutus including officers of the former Hutu Rwandan army have escaped to Kenya from Tingi Tingi in the last two weeks by air at a cost of $800 per seat, Hutu sources say.
The Hutus were fleeing rebels of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire. Rwandan Hutu soldiers have fought alongside Zaire's troops in the east.
But exiled Hutu said many no longer wanted to take part in a war they regarded as Zaire's and wanted to settle elsewhere.
On Wednesday, officials of Zaire's Cizarail train company in Kinshasa said they suspended all traffic to Kindu and evacuated staff and equipment in case of rebel attack.
Cizarail sources said the town was deserted on Tuesday and its residents had fled.
Kindu is 80 km (50 miles) from the town of Kalima, which fell to the rebels last Sunday.

The rebels have seized a stretch of eastern Zaire more than 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October. Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels but all three countries denied any such involvement.
